title: Maharashtra's Varkari
hook: the walk is over, the line to the god stretches out of sight, and some pilgrims bow to the temple's spire and turn for home

segments.voice: Last week ended with Maharashtra's Varkari and its singers: Janabai at the grindstone, Chokhamela outside the walls. Which dull job did you hum through? Day one thousand three hundred eighty-seven.

After all those days of walking, the town comes into view. Pandharpur, on the bank of the river. The dindis pour in, the palkhis arrive, and the singing gets louder, not softer. Then the walkers see the line to stand before Vitthal. It winds through the streets and out of sight. Some will wait in it for many hours. And some, the story of the road says, walk down to the river, bathe, look up at the temple's spire, bow, and turn for home, content. Today, the end of the road, and what counts as arriving.
screen: `PANDHARPUR COMES INTO VIEW.` → `A LINE OUT OF SIGHT.` → `A BOW TO THE SPIRE.`

segments.voice: The river at Pandharpur is the Bhima, and here Varkaris call it the Chandrabhaga, because, tradition says, it bends like a crescent moon. Pilgrims bathe in it first. Then the town fills with singing all through the night, and on the holy day itself, the Ekadashi, the crowd reaches its peak. Inside the temple, Vitthal stands on his brick, hands on hips, the way Pundalik left him. And here's a detail Varkaris treasure: pilgrims are allowed to come close enough to lay their heads on his feet. Not only see him from a distance. Touch. A child running to a mother doesn't stop at arm's length. But the line is long, and not everyone reaches the feet. So Varkari tradition holds that seeing the kalas, the temple's pinnacle, from outside is darshan too, a true seeing of the god. That's the fork in the road at Pandharpur, and the tradition makes room for both. There's one more place on the way in. At the temple's entrance is a step called Namdev's step. Tradition says Namdev asked to be laid there, so that every pilgrim's feet would touch him on the way to Vitthal. And nearby, tradition places Chokhamela's samadhi, the singer who stood outside the walls, now resting at the door. So the road ends the way it began. The saints are already there, under the feet of the crowd, still pointing in. And then the last part. The walkers go home. Back to fields and shops and kitchens, until the next wari. The arriving was never meant to be the whole of it. This was our week with Maharashtra's Varkari. Tomorrow we travel far north, to Kashmir.
screen: `A BATH IN THE CHANDRABHAGA` · `A HEAD ON VITTHAL'S FEET` · `THE SPIRE IS DARSHAN TOO` · `NAMDEV'S STEP, THEN HOME`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath slow. Think back over something you've been working toward for a long time, a road you're still on. Now let yourself stop for a moment, as if you'd just seen the spire from the riverbank. Notice where you are, right now, without needing to be any closer. Then, when the bell nears, gently turn for home, back to your day. If you pray, you can bow inwardly, from wherever you're standing. The bell holds the time.
Maharashtra's Varkari. The walkers who reach Pandharpur, bow at Vitthal's feet or to his spire, step over Namdev's step, and go home until the next wari. Today's word.
Your line: Maharashtra's Varkari. Today, when you finish something, pause once to mark that you've arrived before you rush on. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-seven.

notes: The Bhima called Chandrabhaga at Pandharpur 'because it bends like a crescent moon': a traditional explanation, given as 'tradition says'; confirm.
Pilgrims touching Vitthal's feet (pada-sparsha darshan) and kalas/shikhar darshan counting as darshan: confirm phrasing.
Namdev's step (Namdev Payari) and Chokhamela's samadhi near the temple entrance: told as tradition; confirm.
The wari peaks on Ashadhi Ekadashi; the script says only 'the Ekadashi' to avoid naming dates. A Keeper may want the month named.
Fork 'answer' is the third option (both count), reflecting tradition rather than a single choice.
